subject: Art & Design
title: Design Briefs: Define Before You Design
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Design Briefs: Define Before You Design.

hook.text: A designer who starts without a brief is a ship without a compass. You'll sail, but where?

buildup.text: A design brief captures: the problem, the audience, constraints, deliverables, and success metrics.

discovery.text: The brief protects both designer and client. It sets expectations and prevents scope creep.

twist.text: If a client says 'I'll know it when I see it,' the brief isn't done. Push for specificity upfront.

climax.text: Great designers spend more time understanding the problem than creating the solution.

punchline.text: The design starts before the first pixel. It starts with the question.

quiz.question: What does a good design brief prevent?

details.summary: A design brief is a document that defines the project's objectives, audience, constraints, deliverables, and success criteria before any design work begins.
details.whyItMatters: Most design failures aren't design problems — they're brief problems. Unclear objectives produce unclear designs. The brief is where successful design projects are won or lost, long before any pixels are pushed.
takeaways: Briefs define objectives, audience, and constraints upfront
They align designer and client expectations before work begins
Unclear briefs cause most design project failures

faq.question: What should a design brief include?
faq.answer: Project objectives (what problem the design solves), target audience, key message, deliverables and specifications, brand guidelines to follow, budget, timeline, and success metrics. The more specific the brief, the more focused the design and the fewer revision rounds needed.

faq.question: Who writes the design brief — the client or designer?
faq.answer: Ideally, collaboratively. The client provides business context, audience knowledge, and objectives. The designer structures this into a formal brief, asks clarifying questions, and identifies missing information. The best briefs emerge from conversation, not one-sided documentation.
